newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian PM wades through political minefield.
newsitem.headline: Indian PM wades through political minefield.

text.p: India's government crisis may be over for now, but new Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral still finds himself at the centre of a political minefield.

Among the challenges he faces are a relentless series of threats to his job, regional separatism, forcing through a controversial pro-market budget, and handling peace talks with Pakistan, analysts said on Sunday.
A clutch of separatist movements in Kashmir and in four of seven remote northeastern states are high on his agenda.

On Sunday Gujral was visiting Punjab, seeking to ease lingering mistrust of New Delhi among the leaders of the pro-Sikh Akali Dal party in the northern agricultural state, scene of a bloody Sikh revolt in the 1980s.
Delhi's Asian Age newspaper said Gujral's appointment of Bhabani Sengupta, a political and foreign policy expert, as his key adviser, indicated his eagerness to resolve some of these issues.

"Asked to identify the latter, (Sengupta) said the prime minister was particularly concerned about the situation in the northeast and 'might ask me to look into this'", it quoted the former teacher as saying after his appointment on Saturday.
An interior ministry report last week said tribal rebels and Maoist separatists had stepped up attacks on Indian security forces in the states of Assam, Tripura, Manipur and Nagaland.

Gujral visited the state of Jammu and Kashmir last week. On May 12, he is scheduled to meet Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif in Male to discuss a range of issues dogging their ties, including Kashmir, cause of two of their three wars in the last 50 years.

Pakistan says Kashmir will be a core issue for any progress in peace talks with India. India's rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party has led a chorus of protests, shared by other major groups, against any bargaining on Kashmir.

Gujral, a former Marxist turned social democrat, was thrust into power on April 21, after his fractious United Front held a leadership race in which the bigger political heavyweights cancelled each other out.
The tussle was triggered after the Congress party, providing make-or-break support to the United Front, pulled the rug on then prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda on March 30.

Even before he was sworn in, Gujral, a relative lightweight in the United Front, was forced to grapple first with the Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) party of Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, which walked out of the new government in the leadership row.
Then, as he succeeded in persuading the TMC to change its mind last week, the federal police named the head of Gujral's Janata Dal party in a financial scandal.
Newspapers said Laloo Prasad Yadav, who is also the chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, had threatened to bring down Gujral's government if it pressed for his prosecution.

"Of course, in the present circumstances, every controversy has the potential of escalating to proportions that can unsettle the (federal government)," The Pioneer newspaper said. "Bihar Chief Minister Laloo Prasad Yadav is currently in the eye of one such storm."

Adding to Gujral's woes is the pressure from his influential leftist allies in the 15-party United Front coalition to tone down key provisions of Chidambaram's market-friendly budget for 1997/98 (April-March), due for approval by parliament this month.

The communist-led Left Front opposes Gujral's plans to increase the price of petroleum products, a measure needed to bridge a $4.32 billion deficit incurred by state-run oil companies, which sell petroleum products at subsidised prices.
Gujral, however, was not likely to budge on that.

"You cannot go on living with this kind of deficit that you are soon reaching a stage where you do not have the money to buy. I do not want to reach that stage," he told state television in an interview on Friday.
